articles.title: Guy Ritchie turns a historic Dorset airfield into a tourist destination with Spitfire experiences and holiday apartments; neighbours fear it is becoming an 'aviation theme park'
articles.summary: A historic airfield in the Dorset countryside is taking on a new role as a destination for visitors, with filmmaker Guy Ritchie securing permission to
articles.body: A historic airfield in the Dorset countryside is taking on a new role as a destination for visitors, with filmmaker Guy Ritchie securing permission to turn existing buildings into holiday accommodation. The development is part of a wider transformation of Compton Abbas Airfield, where flying experiences, food, drinks and public events have brought a growing number of visitors to the site. Not everyone living nearby has welcomed the changes. Some residents have raised concerns about aircraft noise, increased commercial activity and the effect on the surrounding landscape. The latest planning decision has added another element to a dispute over how far the airfield should develop as a tourist attraction.Guy Ritchie secures approval for two holiday apartments at Compton Abbas AirfieldDorset Council has granted planning permission for two holiday apartments at Compton Abbas Airfield, allowing existing staff accommodation and an office building to be converted for short-term visitor stays. The proposed units will have two and four bedrooms respectively, providing accommodation for people visiting the site and taking part in its aviation activities.As reported by The Sun, the decision gives Ritchie another opportunity to develop the business around the historic airfield without constructing an entirely new accommodation complex. Guests will be able to spend the night at the property and take part in flying experiences during their stay. A planning condition requires the apartments to operate as short-term holiday accommodation rather than permanent homes.The approval also changes the permitted use of buildings that had previously served the airfield's operational needs. The airfield had permission to use a flat for live-in staff dating back to 2005. Residents argued that the original arrangement was intended to ensure someone remained on site for security and safety purposes.How Guy Ritchie transformed a 1961 Dorset airfield into a tourist destinationThe BBC reported in January 2024 that Compton Abbas Airfield first opened in 1961, citing the Airfields of Britain Conservation Trust. For much of its existence, it operated as a relatively modest flying location, serving aviation enthusiasts and private pilots.Ritchie acquired the property in 2022 and began developing its commercial offering. The site now combines aviation-related activities with hospitality and entertainment, attracting people who may not necessarily be visiting to fly an aircraft themselves.Among its attractions are experiences involving historic aircraft, including the opportunity to fly in a Spitfire. The airfield also has a smokehouse restaurant, while visitors can purchase craft beers and ales produced by Ritchie's Gritchie Brewing Company.Its events calendar has expanded too. Classic car gatherings, live music on Fridays and heritage aviation displays have become part of the programme, giving the property a wider appeal beyond its original flying community.The airfield's development has taken place alongside Ritchie's ownership of Ashcombe Estate, which lies close to the Dorset and Wiltshire border. The filmmaker previously shared Ashcombe House with his former wife Madonna. He now divides his time between the countryside property and his London home with his wife, Jacqui. The estate has also provided a setting for visits from well-known figures, including David Beckham and Robert Downey Jr.Residents raise noise and environmental concerns over Compton Abbas AirfieldThe holiday accommodation application has brought existing tensions between the airfield and some nearby residents back into focus. Their objections extend beyond the two apartments, with several arguing that the site's increasing commercial activity is changing the character of an area where development is subject to environmental protections.Compton Abbas Airfield is situated within the Cranborne Chase National Landscape, which is also recognised as an International Dark Sky Reserve. Residents concerned about the changes say the location requires particular care because of its rural character, wildlife and relatively dark night skies.Christopher Dymond, a neighbour, has complained about the frequency of flying activities and the noise generated by historic aircraft. He described the airfield's earlier operation as a small, carefully managed facility serving local flying enthusiasts.In his objection, Dymond said the scale of activity had increased considerably, with events and visitor attractions contributing to disturbances for people living nearby. He also described the experience of spending time in his garden during busy summer weekends, when aircraft regularly pass overhead.Neighbours question holiday lets as airfield expansion fears growResidents argued that the accommodation was approved because a member of staff needed to live on the premises to provide security and respond to safety requirements. They have questioned whether converting the property into holiday accommodation is consistent with the purpose for which the original permission was granted. Dymond also argued that planning arrangements contained provisions requiring the accommodation's use to cease if the operational need for an on-site employee no longer existed.His objection was that replacing staff accommodation with paid visitor stays would change the purpose of the building without addressing the original justification for allowing someone to live there.Philip Cayford, another neighbour and member of the Compton Abbas Airfield Monitoring Group, raised wider concerns about the site's commercial direction. He said the airfield had originally been a private grass strip capable of accommodating around six small aircraft.The phrase 'aviation theme park by stealth' became one of the most prominent descriptions used by opponents of the development. Their argument is that the accumulation of individual attractions and planning permissions is gradually changing the nature of the airfield.Dorset Council says the holiday apartments are acceptableDespite the objections, the council concluded that there were no sufficient planning grounds to reject the application. Planning officer Jamie Francis acknowledged, “The owner has been open that they are seeking to generate additional income streams for the airfield, which would have personal gain, this is also considered to bring economic benefits to the area.”The planning assessment found that converting the existing buildings into tourist accommodation was acceptable in place of their previous uses. It also concluded that the change was unlikely to have a significant effect on neighbouring residents, air pollution or the airfield's normal flying operations. The council's decision was specific to the proposed accommodation. The short-term letting condition means the apartments cannot be used as permanent residential properties under the permission.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Hong Kong democracy campaigner Joshua Wong handed another 10 years in jail
articles.summary: Joshua Wong, once a teenage figurehead of Hong Kong’s democracy movement, faces the prospect of entering middle age in prison, after a court Thursday meted out a 10-year sentence over a second national security conviction.
articles.body: Joshua Wong, once a teenage figurehead of Hong Kong’s democracy movement, faces the prospect of entering middle age in prison, after a court Thursday meted out a 10-year sentence over a second national security conviction. Wong became a prominent activist when he was a teenager, and entered prison for the first time at 23. He turned 30 last month. In September, he pleaded guilty to conspiring with fellow activists to invite foreign sanctions against China and Hong Kong in 2020 – the year Beijing introduced the city’s National Security Law (NSL), which led to a crackdown on dissent, the shuttering of vocal news outlets, and the dissolution of civic groups. Wong is already serving 4 years and 8 months in prison, after pleading guilty in a landmark subversion trial in 2024. He was due for release in January. Beijing imposed the NSL on Hong Kong after huge and often violent pro-democracy protests convulsed the international financial hub in 2019. The law tightened Beijing’s grip on the former British colony. Both the Hong Kong and Chinese governments say it has helped restore stability, but rights groups say the law has stifled dissent and made any criticism of the government risky. Calling Wong’s case “grave,” Judge William Tam said the activist conspired with others – including Nathan Law, a former legislator now living in self-exile overseas – to call for foreign sanctions at a time when Hong Kong was dealing with its own social turmoil, referring to the anti-government protests. After the NSL came in, the judge said, Wong and his conspirators “continued to promote such calls not only through their own social media accounts but also via prominent news media or outlets in the West, reaching both local and international audience.” “Whilst it is a very heavy sentence on the defendant, the punishment must fit the gravity of the crime committed,” he said, adding that it’s “also necessary for this court to express the community’s abhorrence” at Wong’s actions. In his mitigation letter, viewed by CNN, Wong wrote that his activism “was never driven by hatred.” He’s been spending his spare time in jail studying the law and keeping abreast of technological advances, including artificial intelligence, he said. “Yet none of my aspirations for the future is more important than my solemn wish to care for my ageing parents once I complete my sentence,” he wrote. China’s leaders have previously labeled Wong and other activists “separatists.” In the latest case, prosecutors accused Wong of conspiring with others to lobby the United States and other countries to sanction China and Hong Kong, prior to the NSL’s imposition. This, they said, happened through social media campaigning, as well as meetings with US politicians, including former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi and then Senator Marco Rubio, now the US secretary of state. The lobbying continued after the law was enacted, prosecutors said, with the US sanctioning more than a dozen Hong Kong and Chinese officials after 2020. A Hong Kong government spokesperson earlier dismissed international criticism of Wong’s prosecution. “The lawful exercise of free speech must not be conflated with taking actions to collude with a foreign country to impose ‘sanctions’ to harm one’s own country,” they said in September. Speaking after the sentence was announced, Hong Kong Chief Executive John Lee, a former top security official, said Wong and Law committed “extremely serious offences, which not only severely undermined national sovereignty, security, and development interests, but also directly prejudiced the well-being of the general public and the stability of society.” Face of a movement Ahead of the sentencing Thursday morning, police had heightened security outside the court near Hong Kong’s financial district, where dozens of people had camped out – some for two nights – to catch a glimpse of one of the city’s most famous prisoners. Among them was housewife ET Wong, who said she had started following Wong’s campaigning when he was still an adolescent. “He chose a difficult path for the future, human rights and student movements of Hong Kong,” she said. “He should not have been in jail for one single day.” Activist Lui Yuk-lin held a card with Wong’s name on it as she entered the building, lamenting the fate of the former teen figurehead. “He’s a child in my heart,” she said. When he was led into court, Wong, wearing a navy shirt and his usual black-framed glasses, nodded to supporters in the public gallery. Given the limited space, well-wishers took turns filing through the gallery. Letters from prison Weeks after pleading guilty to his second national security charge in September, Wong – who’s been behind bars since 2020 – told his friend in a letter that he had been feeling “so-so.” “[It’s] very difficult to describe the feeling and thought,” Wong wrote in the letter, shared with CNN by his friend. But the former activist also encouraged his friend to stay positive, citing a verse from the Bible. “There is no fear in love,” Wong wrote, quoting from The First Epistle of John, adding that the fear he had experienced over the past few years made him appreciate his love for his friends and the city even more. Louis Lee, who shared his exchanges with Wong, said they discussed everything from music to their favourite Japanese anime, and would reminiscence about good times. Reading Wong’s letters sometimes brought Lee to tears. “As a friend, I miss him so much and I long to see the day when he’s out of the prison,” Lee said. The skinny, bespectacled activist with a knack for fiery public speaking rose to prominence in 2012 at the age of 15, leading sit-in protests with his friends to successfully overturn a government plan to introduce Chinese civic education to the city’s schools. At the time, critics feared the proposed curriculum amounted to propaganda by Beijing. Under the NSL, it’s now compulsory in every school. Two years later, Wong became one of the key leaders of the city’s Umbrella Movement protests that rallied thousands of predominantly young people to the streets to call for greater democracy by blocking major thoroughfares for 79 straight days. In 2016, he co-founded pro-democracy party Demosisto, which successfully sent co-founder Law to the city’s Legislative Council as its youngest member (Wong was too young to run.) The party announced its disbandment hours after Beijing passed the NSL, with Law revealing days later he had left Hong Kong. Law is now one of dozens of democracy activists overseas wanted by Hong Kong’s national security police, and who have had a cash bounty put on them. Authorities disqualified Wong when he tried to run again in 2020. He was later arrested and charged along with dozens of others for taking part in unofficial primaries held to screen candidates for Legislative Council elections. In what was widely known as the “47 case,” after the number of opposition figures on trial, prosecutors said Wong and others subverted the Hong Kong government in 2020 by engaging in a primary election – a common practice in many democracies. At the time, Hong Kong authorities said the primary vote was a “vicious plot” intended to “paralyze the government and undermine state power,” and accused those who took part of intending to use their mandate to block legislation indiscriminately. Of the 47, most pleaded guilty while 14 were convicted and sentenced to up to 10 years in prison, after a 2024 trial that marked the single largest prosecution of pro-democracy activists under the NSL. Two were acquitted. Since the NSL came into effect, civil groups have disbanded, and some independent media outlets have been shut down. The city’s legislature now comprises only pro-Beijing loyalists, while most pro-democracy figures are either in jail or in exile overseas.

articles.title: Delhi pollution worsens, AQI hits 482 as 7 stations record severe levels
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Delhi's air quality remained in the severe category on Thursday morning, with the overall Air Quality Index (AQI) touching 482 at 8.01am.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Delhi's air quality remained in the severe category on Thursday morning, with the overall Air Quality Index (AQI) touching 482 at 8.01am. Several parts of the national capital continued to record high pollution levels.According to Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) data, seven monitoring stations recorded AQI levels above 400, falling in the severe category.Punjabi Bagh recorded the highest AQI at 446, followed by Narela at 434, Rohini at 431, RK Puram at 416, Bawana at 412, North Campus, Delhi University, at 408 and Patparganj at 405.Several other areas reported very poor air quality. Okhla Phase-2 and India Gate both recorded an AQI of 399, followed by ITO at 397, Dwarka Sector 8 at 396, Chandni Chowk at 356 and Vasundhara Enclave at 330.Anand Vihar recorded an AQI of 293, while the IMD Lodhi Road station reported 268. Both stations fell in the poor category.Amid the deterioration in Delhi's air quality, Union Environment Minister Bhupender Yadav said on Tuesday that the Centre's air quality panel was continuously monitoring meteorological conditions, including wind direction, wind speed and the movement of air. He also assured that necessary action was being taken.The worsening air quality comes despite a decline in stubble-burning incidents compared to previous years. The government has claimed that a significant portion of paddy stubble has been utilised through ex-situ management.Asked about the reduction in stubble-burning incidents in neighbouring states, including Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh, Yadav said, “Yes, I have already stated that around 40 per cent of the paddy stubble has been utilised through ex-situ management this time."Responding to reporter’s question on why air quality continues to remain in the severe category despite these measures, Yadav said the Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM) was closely monitoring meteorological conditions and taking necessary steps based on its assessments.“CAQM is continuously monitoring meteorological conditions, including wind direction, wind speed and the movement of air. Based on these assessments, the necessary steps are being taken,” he said.Dr Saurabh Mittal, Assistant Professor in the Department of Pulmonary, Critical Care and Sleep Medicine at AIIMS, Delhi, said, "Since AQI has increased, we are seeing patients who have prior respiratory problems, but now they are coming with increased symptoms and exacerbations, for which we need to increase their medications, like their inhaler doses have to be increased, and some patients need the addition of new medications such as oral steroids also to reduce their cough. We are also seeing patients who have previously been asymptomatic, but now, because of the increased pollution, they are developing respiratory symptoms in terms of cough, irritation of the throat, nasal irritation, and shortness of breath. So those patients also need some kind of treatment or decongestants for symptom relief... There has been an increase in people actually calling us... I would say that we anticipate that this number is probably going to increase in the next couple of weeks..."Explaining the factors contributing to the pollution, Mittal said, "It's a multifactorial problem. It's not a one-time or one-day problem. Of course, weather contributes significantly to it; as the winter weather appears, the condensation happens. Of course, vehicular emissions, construction, stubble burning - all of these things contribute to a larger extent. But individual contribution is very difficult to kind of quantify. But yes, if we reduce all of them, it's likely that we'll have some relief from the problem."(With Agency Inputs)You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Delhi | Silver Rate in Delhi | Bank Holidays in Delhi | Public Holidays in Delhi | Delhi AQI | Weather in Delhi | Petrol Price in Delhi | Diesel Price in Delhi | CNG Price in Delhi | LPG Price in DelhiStay updated with the latest Delhi news. articles.title: Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong sentenced to 10 years in prison in 2nd national security case
articles.summary: Wong, 30, who is already serving a four-year, eight-month prison term, had been expected to be freed in January 2027.
articles.body: HONG KONG — Prominent Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong was sentenced to 10 years in prison Thursday for his second conviction under a Beijing-imposed national security law, in a case that critics say reflects the crackdown on the Chinese territory’s once-thriving pro-democracy movement. Wong was charged in 2025 with conspiracy to collude with foreign forces to endanger national security under the law. In September, he pleaded guilty to the offense, a move that can typically reduce the sentence. Wong, 30, is already serving a four-year, eight-month prison term for the city’s biggest national security case linked to an unofficial primary after entering a guilty plea in that case. Before being prosecuted for the collusion-related charge, Wong had been expected to be freed in January 2027. Judge William Tam said during the sentencing hearing that Wong’s offense was of a grave nature and rejected that his role was limited. He also said he considered a 13-year prison sentence as a starting point but reduced it because of Wong’s guilty plea. Wong looked calm and thanked his supporters before leaving the court. His supporters waved to him, and Tiffany Chin, a former member of the now-disbanded Scholarism, once led by Wong, was in tears. The judge said Wong could serve his two prison sentences concurrently. Wong has only about two months left on the sentence for his previous national security conviction. Resident ET Wong said that when Joshua Wong was just a teenager, he possessed “big-picture thinking” that some adults might not even have. He walked a difficult path for Hong Kong’s future, human rights and student movement, she said. “At least in my heart, he should not have spent a single day in wrongful imprisonment,” she said. Wong’s convictions seen as discouraging dissent Hong Kong once had a freewheeling civil society marked by its vibrant protest and media scenes. But after an anti-government movement rocked the city in 2019, authorities reduced public choice in elections and arrested many leading activists. Some news outlets known for their reports critical of the government shut down, and dozens of civil society groups dissolved. Observers say Wong’s sentencing shows the authorities’ determination to keep prominent activists in prison for as long as possible, further chilling civic activism. “NSL charges can be repeatedly weaponized to keep a specific political prisoner in jail, if the government deems necessary,” said Eric Lai, a research fellow at the Georgetown Center for Asian Law, referring to the national security law. But Beijing views Wong as an anti-China figure supporting Hong Kong independence, a stance that crosses its red line. Hong Kong authorities also say the security law was crucial for the city’s stability following monthslong anti-government protests in 2019, maintaining that the city’s law enforcement actions are evidence-based. Prosecution highlights Wong’s lobbying and advocacy efforts The prosecution previously alleged that Wong and fellow activist Nathan Law had agreed in or around 2016 to lobby internationally to achieve their goal of democratic self-determination. It said that before the security law was introduced, the pair had been calling for sanctions and other adverse measures against Hong Kong and China. It pointed to his meetings with U.S. politicians such as Nancy Pelosi and Marco Rubio in 2016 and 2019. After the law was enacted, Law and others advanced their work abroad by meeting foreign politicians and launching petition drives, it said. Wong supported the effort from Hong Kong through foreign media outlets and social media to draw foreign countries’ attention and bolster the request for sanctions, blockade or other hostile measures against China and Hong Kong, it said. His lawyer Derek Chan earlier urged the court to impose a sentence that would give his client some hope, adding that Wong wishes to take care of his parents after his release. His friends said that during his nearly six years in prison, Wong has kept busy reading books and exercising, teaching himself guitar while maturing in his thinking. To his supporters, Wong is a political star representing a younger generation born in the final years of Hong Kong’s British colonial rule before the city’s return to China in 1997. Despite being held behind bars, Wong’s influence appears to have remained a concern, at least for the pro-Beijing camp. In September, a pro-Beijing newspaper report criticized a 2017 documentary about Wong on Netflix for “beautifying” his crimes. The city’s security bureau told local media the government was taking follow-up action. The documentary then shot to the top of Netflix’s popular chart in Hong Kong.

articles.title: Syria, Saudi Arabia sign defence cooperation deal, agree $403m in loans
articles.summary: Defence cooperation deal signed as Syria’s President al-Sharaa visits Riyadh for the second time in less than a month.
articles.body:
Syria’s President Ahmed al-Sharaa and Saudi Arabia’s Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman have overseen the signing of several agreements, including a defence cooperation deal, and more than $403m in Saudi loans for Syria’s energy, housing, health and infrastructure sectors.

The agreements were signed on Wednesday, during al-Sharaa’s second visit to Riyadh in less than a month.

Syria’s Foreign Ministry called the cooperation agreement between the two countries’ defence ministries the “most notable” of the deals. But it did not disclose the terms.

The defence agreement came days after Syria’s Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani said his government was weighing whether to join a mutual defence pact among Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan.

“Discussions are currently under way to evaluate Syria’s entry into the Mecca alliance,” al-Shaibani said on Saturday at the Manama Dialogue, a security conference in Bahrain.

Saudi Arabia has sought help from the United States and countries in Europe and the Middle East for both defensive and offensive support, in a renewed war against the Houthis in Yemen. The group has attacked airports and oil facilities in Saudi Arabia as it fights forces aligned with Yemen’s internationally recognised government for control of the country.

In its statement on X, the Syrian Foreign Ministry said al-Sharaa and Prince Mohammed had discussed the “current regional and international situation” during their talks in Riyadh.

That included the effects of military escalation on regional security, the safety of international shipping, the reliability of energy supplies and the stability of the global economy, it said.

The two men called for de-escalation and the peaceful resolution of disputes. They also urged an “immediate cessation of all actions that threaten the security of maritime navigation” in the Red Sea, the Bab al-Mandeb strait and the Strait of Hormuz, the statement added.

Syrian political researcher Ahmed Qassem told Al Jazeera that al-Sharaa’s “second visit in such a short time indicates the magnitude of the security challenges in the region” as well as in Syria. He argued that Syria should join the Mecca alliance, as the country needs a “deterrence force” to protect its sovereignty and to deter increasing Israeli encroachment on its territory.

During al-Sharaa’s visit, the Saudi Fund for Development also agreed to provide $403m in loans under six agreements with Syria’s Finance Ministry, on concessional terms, the official Saudi Press Agency reported.

They include $100m to rebuild and equip damaged healthcare facilities, $60m to repair damaged housing, $105m to strengthen civil defence, $90m to rehabilitate the Aleppo thermal power plant and $30m to develop drinking water systems in Damascus and Idlib, the agency said.

The two governments also signed a memorandum of understanding on industrial cooperation and two more on agriculture and environmental protection, it added.

Saudi Arabia has been a key backer of Syria’s government since al-Sharaa came to power after the overthrow of Bashar al-Assad in December 2024. The two leaders last met in Riyadh on October 6.

According to the Syrian presidency, they discussed plans for Syria’s reconstruction at that meeting, including rebuilding damaged infrastructure and essential facilities.

articles.body: The Pentagon’s technology chief Emil Michael has said the United States was unprepared for the rise of modern drone warfare and admitted that Ukraine had to develop some of the battlefield technologies it needed because the US could not provide them. Speaking at the WSJ Tech Conference, Michael said the conflict between Ukraine and Russia exposed significant gaps in America's military preparedness and accelerated efforts to expand the country's drone capabilities.Pentagon CTO: We were caught flat-footedAddressing the conference in Napa, California, Michael said the Pentagon had not anticipated how central drones would become to modern warfare. "We were caught flat-footed by the drone warfare in Ukraine and Russia," he said, adding that the US was not prepared because it "just didn't imagine it." He said the Defence Department is now focused on preparing for future conflicts and anticipating how warfare could evolve.Michael acknowledged that while the United States provided substantial support to Ukraine during its war with Russia, Ukrainian forces often had to create their own solutions on the battlefield. "We helped the Ukrainians a ton, but they invented what they actually needed because we didn't have it," he said.Stockpile growth, but Ukraine far aheadMichael said the US built about 1,000 drones under the previous administration, while its stockpile is now around 500,000. That is still a small fraction of the eight million to 10 million drones Ukraine estimates it will build this year, as its war with Russia nears a fifth year. Michael said the US helped Ukraine a great deal, but Ukrainian forces invented the technology they needed because the US did not have it.Pentagon studying future battlefieldsMichael said the Defence Department's Project Meridian has been tasked with examining what future warfare could look like, including potential conflicts underground and in space. The initiative includes participation from industry figures such as Elon Musk, chief executive of SpaceX, and Palmer Luckey, founder of Anduril IndustriesCautious on AI targetingEven as the Pentagon pushes into cheap, autonomous systems, Michael said the military remains conservative about using artificial intelligence in combat. Developing targets still depends more on intelligence reports, satellite imagery and other human-led investigation than on AI, he said, adding that the US is not very sophisticated at AI-generated targeting.Michael declined to comment on the US strike in Iran last February that hit a girls’ school the US had mistaken for a military target. More than 100 people were killed, including dozens of children. The US has not released the findings of its investigation, and planning for the strike involved an AI targeting system. Michael said there must be appropriate human judgment at every level.Reiterates criticism of AnthropicMichael also reiterated his criticism of AI company Anthropic, which the Defence Department earlier designated as a national security threat. He said it was not difficult for the Pentagon to stop using Anthropic's models and noted that the department continues to use AI models from Google, OpenAI and Grok on its networks.US still ahead of China in AIOn the global AI race, Michael argued that the United States maintains an advantage over China thanks to its access to advanced semiconductors and greater data-centre capacity.According to Michael, Beijing remains approximately six months to a year behind the United States in AI development, although he indicated that competition between the two countries remains intense.You use AI every day. articles.title: Multiple grizzlies may have attacked mother and daughter found dead, Canadian authorities say
articles.summary: More than one grizzly may have been involved in a bear attack that relatives say left a mother and daughter dead in Bella Coola along the province’s central coast, the Conservation Officer Service in British Columbia said.
articles.body: More than one grizzly may have been involved in a bear attack that relatives say left a mother and daughter dead in Bella Coola along the province’s central coast, the Conservation Officer Service in British Columbia said. The service’s Inspector Jeff Tyre said in a video message that the second body had been found in a search by Royal Canadian Mounted Police and conservation officers on Tuesday afternoon that followed the discovery of the first set of remains a day earlier. He said it’s “not yet clear if more than one bear was involved,” and any bears captured in the area will be assessed. Family members of art therapist Jenny Balcarras and her daughter, Selah Reed, had reported them missing on Sunday. Balcarras’ brother, Matthew Balcarras, said Wednesday that his sister was “incredibly strong” and had lived in many difficult, remote places, including Alaska, before moving to Bella Coola on B.C.’s central coast a few months ago. “She was a beautiful artist and was an inspiration for me and my brothers,” Matthew Balcarras said of his sister. Authorities have imposed a curfew on the community, about 1,000 kilometres north of Vancouver, as the search for the animal or animals behind the attack continues. If the “offending bear” is captured it will be killed to protect public safety, Tyre said. A fundraiser set up by relative Mary Melissa Smith said Reed was 20, “with her whole life ahead of her,” while Balcarras leaves behind three young adult children, as well as a grandchild. Balcarras left behind a son, two daughters and a grandson who now are “faced with the devastating loss of their mother,” while navigating the financial burden of arranging funeral services, Smith said. The Central Coast Teachers’ Association said on social media that Balcarras had joined their school community as a counselor in August, and she devoted “countless hours to connecting with the students she served and worked closely with teachers and other staff supporting their well-being.” The attack comes nearly a year after a grizzly attack on a group of 20 elementary school students and teachers in the same area, which left one adult and three children badly hurt. The animal involved in that attack last November was never captured. Kim Titchener, founder of Bear Safety & More Inc. based in Calgary, said she was concerned when she saw reports about the women on Facebook hiking groups. “When I saw that they were missing and in the area that they were missing, my heart just dropped because I just kind of knew this could be a bear attack,” Titchener said. “This community and area have suffered so much last year,” she said, referring to the grizzly attack on schoolchildren. Bella Coola is well-known for its large population of grizzly and black bears, and Titchener said it’s common for people in Bella Coola to see bears walking near their homes. Titchener said there have been “concerning pressures” on bear populations in British Columbia because of the loss of habitat, food stress caused by drought and climate change, setting off more conflicts with people. “I don’t know if Bella Coola suffered from any drought issues, but certainly other parts of the province of B.C. did,” she said.

articles.title: Zelenskyy hopes Democratic Congress will bring more US help for Ukraine
articles.summary: EU officials also urge new US Congress to step up pressure on Russia to end the four-and-a-half-year war.
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has expressed hope that Democratic gains in the United States midterm ⁠elections will bring ⁠more help for Kyiv, as European officials urged the new US Congress to ramp up pressure on Russia to end Europe’s bloodiest conflict since World War II.

Zelenskyy’s comments on Wednesday came after American voters rebuked US President Donald Trump and his Republican Party, handing control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives to the Democratic Party.

In an interview with German broadcaster ZDF, Zelenskyy said the Democratic gains could work to Ukraine’s advantage.

“I am also grateful to the Republicans, but the Democrats speak very clearly about supporting Ukraine and providing assistance to Ukraine,” Zelenskyy said. “They speak about renewing the connection between the United States and Europe… Therefore, there is hope that a balance of power will emerge, and that we will receive more support.”

Zelenskyy said more US aid could have an effect ‌on Russian President Vladimir Putin.

“If Congress now speaks of strong financial support or military assistance, as Europe is doing and demonstrating today, then that will be something positive that will have an impact on Putin,” he told ZDF.

Zelenskyy has worked to repair a rocky relationship with Trump since an Oval Office meeting in February 2025 at which the US president accused his Ukrainian counterpart of being “ungrateful” for Washington’s aid.

In recent weeks, Trump has made several moves favourable to Russia, including a deal to import Russian diesel.

Last month, he waived sanctions on Russia that Congress had overwhelmingly approved as part of legislation supporting Ukraine.

Ukraine has also accused Washington of delaying deliveries of interceptor missiles.

Kaja Kallas, the European Union’s foreign policy chief, said she hoped the new Congress would “continue supporting Ukraine and also putting more pressure on Russia”.

“Europe as well as US, we are much stronger together,” Kallas said, expressing hope that joint pressure would force Moscow to end the war.

In Germany, leaders were divided. Chancellor Friedrich Merz expressed scepticism on Wednesday that Trump would change course despite the Democrats’ sweeping victory.

“Quite frankly, over the last two years, Trump has largely governed by bypassing Congress. Why should that be any different now?” Merz said at an event in Berlin, a day after US voters handed Republicans a historic defeat.

His foreign minister, Johann Wadephul, was more hopeful. He said the “very clear” Democratic victory could create “a new opportunity to launch a fresh initiative” to end the wars in Ukraine and Iran. He added that he was “quite optimistic” that aid to Ukraine, which has been slashed under Trump, would get “more discussion” from US lawmakers of both parties.

Others in Europe cautioned that with Trump in office for two more years, Washington’s foreign policy was unlikely to change quickly.

The US president has berated European leaders, roiled their economies with tariffs, threatened to pull the US out of NATO , and said he wants to take over Greenland, a semiautonomous territory of Denmark.

“Our security and prosperity in Austria and Europe must not depend on how people in Kansas or Iowa vote,” Austria’s foreign minister, Beate Meinl-Reisinger, said. “That’s why we are strengthening our own defence capability and our own competitiveness.”

In Moscow, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Russia hoped Trump “will continue his peacemaking efforts”, regardless of the election result.

Democratic aides have told US media that helping Kyiv would be a priority when the party takes control of the congressional agenda in January. But diplomacy is moving faster.

Steve Witkoff, Trump’s envoy, said Washington would bring Ukrainian and Russian delegations together in Abu Dhabi on November 10 and 11 to discuss ending the war and security arrangements for Ukraine.

Zelenskyy said on Wednesday that he has had detailed conversations with Witkoff and Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, ahead of the meeting.

“The negotiations must move forward at full throttle to bring this war to an end as quickly as possible. Ukraine is ready to take the necessary steps,” he wrote on X.

articles.title: Bob Dylan comes knockin’ on pope’s door as Leo welcomes legend to Vatican
articles.summary: Leo had quoted from an unpublished protest song Dylan penned in 1963, “Go Away You Bomb,” in his 2026 book.
articles.body: VATICAN CITY — Bob Dylan came knockin’ on Pope Leo XIV’s door Wednesday, as the American singer-songwriter and poet visited with the American pope at the Vatican during a break between concert dates in Italy. The Vatican said the encounter was brief, with Leo giving Dylan a rosary and Dylan presenting the pope with a copy of his autobiography, “Chronicles: Volume One.” Leo had quoted from an unpublished protest song Dylan penned in 1963, “Go Away You Bomb,” in his 2026 book “Disarmed and Disarming: Peace Is a Gift.” Leo was warning against the race to rearm and the recourse to nuclear weapons and quoted the lyric, addressed to a hypothetical atomic bomb: “I hate you cause yer man-made and man-owned, an’ man-handled.” Two Vatican officials accompanied Dylan: the Rev. Antonio Spadaro, a Vatican culture ministry official who also accompanied Patti Smith to a July audience with Leo; and Andrea Monda, the editor of the Vatican newspaper, L’Osservatore Romano. Spadaro said Dylan had wanted to speak with Leo, and the two met in private for a few minutes. In an essay in L'Osservatore Romano, he recalled that the former Robert Prevost, who was born in Chicago in 1955, grew up familiar with Dylan's music. He also noted that Dylan was very familiar with St. Augustine of Hippo, the inspiration of Leo's spirituality and Augustinian religious order, penning “I Dreamed I Saw St. Augustine” for the 1967 album “John Wesley Harding.” Dylan, who won the Nobel Prize for Literature in 2016, wore a black hoodie and a loose tie. Vatican photos of the encounter showed him with the hood over his head. It wasn’t Dylan’s first papal encounter: He played for Pope John Paul II, and thousands of other people, in 1997 during a concert capping a religious congress in Bologna, Italy. Dylan, who changed his name from Robert Zimmerman, was born to a Jewish family in Minnesota. He famously became a born-again Christian in 1979 and alienated some of his longtime fans with songs like “Gotta Serve Somebody” and “Saved.” In more recent years, Dylan has been more circumspect about his religious beliefs. In a 2022 interview with The Wall Street Journal, Dylan said that he was a “religious person” who reads the Scriptures, meditates and prays. Dylan met with Leo between concert dates in Italy. He played in Milan on Monday and is playing Rome on Thursday. In his most recent concert before the meeting with the pope, Dylan sang his 1997 song “Tryin’ to Get to Heaven” that contains the lyric “I’ve been all around the world, boys/Now I’m trying to get to heaven before they close the door."

articles.title: Trump said he’d accept the election results. Netanyahu is challenging the outcome of his.
articles.summary: As Republican losses in the US midterm elections came into focus, President Donald Trump said he would accept the results. The same cannot be said of Benjamin Netanyahu, the man Trump endorsed in Israel.
articles.body: As Republican losses in the US midterm elections came into focus, President Donald Trump said he would accept the results. The same cannot be said of Benjamin Netanyahu, the man Trump endorsed in Israel. A week after Israel’s October 27 election, Netanyahu, whose bloc lost its majority, is still challenging the officially certified results. He and his Likud party allege, without presenting evidence, that the vote was “stolen” by Israel’s Arab parties and foreign actors. The post-election dispute deepened this week after the David Zini, chief of the Shin Bet internal security service and a Netanyahu loyalist, pushed to investigate the leaders of the Arab parties. The attorney general, a longtime target of Israel’s right-wing, refused to authorize such an investigation without evidence. “Likud and Netanyahu are trying to commit a pogrom against democracy and the rule of law,” Gadi Eisenkot, Netanyahu’s main rival, said Tuesday. One day later, Netanyahu doubled down on his claims of fraud. “There are serious suspicions that foreign countries have been involved, using enormous sums of money, in an attempt to manipulate the results of the elections in the State of Israel,” he said in a video statement. The official results show Netanyahu’s bloc plummeted from a commanding 68 to 53 of the 120 seats in the Knesset, or parliament. The opposition, led by Eisenkot, holds 67 seats. But nearly a third of those comes from the two Arab parties, the Joint List and Raam, after a historic turnout that secured 19 seats. The Arab parties’ support is decisive to any effort to replace Netanyahu. That is why undermining their legitimacy has become the focus of Netanyahu’s post-election strategy. Since the results came in, Netanyahu and his right-wing allies have been propagating claims that the election was “stolen” by the Arab parties through bribery, foreign funding and fraud. A day after the vote, Likud submitted hundreds of testimonies to the Central Elections Committee demanding investigations and arrests. Over the weekend, Netanayhu shared a video on social media of a right-wing activist claiming massive forgeries and calling to “simply invalidate the elections.” The committee has rejected claims of widespread fraud as baseless, saying there is no evidentiary basis to allege systematic compromise of the vote. The committee did, however, ask the Shin Bet last week to examine “serious suspicions” of foreign funding intended to influence the campaign. In a letter leaked to Israeli media, committee chair Justice Noam Sohlberg cautioned that he could not verify the seriousness of the material. But Netanyahu’s Likud party treated the letter as a confirmation of the broader fraud narrative. Sohlberg appeared alongside the Shin Bet chief and Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara to make an unusual joint statement Sunday in which they assured the public that the elections were conducted properly. They said that even if the foreign funding suspicions were substantiated, it wouldn’t overturn the result or undermine the integrity of the process. But Zini’s subsequent conduct has escalated the controversy. A retired Israel Defense Forces major general who describes himself as a “proud messianic,” Zini was appointed by Netanyahu last year from outside the Shin Bet ranks. He is now reportedly seeking to question four senior Arab political figures, including several party leaders. The Shin Bet told the committee Wednesday that its intelligence “seemingly” points to “extensive phenomena” of large sums being funneled into Israel from foreign sources “on a scale exceeding thousands of people and possibly even more,” according to a source briefed on the matter. The agency said further investigation was needed before it could point “with a high level of certainty” to the scope. But the Shin Bet presented no public evidence. In a rare statement Tuesday, the attorney general’s office said Zini had prevented the Shin Bet from passing any pertinent evidence to her office or to the police. “In a state governed by law, citizens or elected officials cannot be investigated without evidence justification,” it said. “Anyone who needs to be questioned will be, but no one will be investigated without evidentiary grounds.” The Likud party, in response, accused Baharav-Miara of obstructing the investigation. Netanyahu’s far-right ally, Itamar Ben Gvir, called on Zini to arrest and investigate the Arab leaders even without the attorney general’s approval. The clash feeds into an ongoing conflict: Netanyahu’s outgoing government voted to dismiss Baharav-Miara in August 2025, but the Supreme Court blocked the move. Since then, the government has repeatedly challenged and defied her directives. The Arab parties rejected the allegations, accusing Zini of participating in the Likud’s campaign to delegitimize the Arab public, their votes and their record political representation. “Netanyahu is clinging to power and trying to deny the legitimacy of the Arab public which voted en masse and decided against his government. Zini, appointed by Netanyahu, is acting as a political arm in his service,” the Joint List said in a statement. Mansour Abbas, chairman of Raam, called the move an “an unacceptable attempt to tarnish the Arab public.” Opposition leaders, who are now making plans to use their Knesset majority to replace the body’s speaker, accuse Netanyahu and Zini of dragging Israel into a constitutional crisis and eroding trust in the election. Eisenkot called the moment a test for Israel’s future “as a liberal democratic state.” He urged security and law enforcement officials to remember they “are servants of the kingdom, not the king.” Former Prime Minister Yair Lapid called it an “attempt to crush democracy and steal the elections with the help of regime loyalists planted in the security system.” Yair Golan, chairman of the left-wing Democrats party, said Zini has turned the Shin Bet into “a political tool in service of Netanyahu’s campaign to undermine the election results.” The political test will come in the weeks ahead. If Netanyahu persuades right-wing parties and potential individual defectors in the opposition that relying on Arab parties is illegitimate, he may block the only path to his ouster. But his tactics could also push the divided opposition to come together and hasten the outcome he is seeking to prevent.

articles.title: Bangladesh garment factories close as workers clash with police in pay protests
articles.summary: Workers are demanding a minimum monthly wage of $245, up from $100, saying rising living costs and inflation have eroded their purchasing power.
articles.body: DHAKA, Bangladesh — Police in Bangladesh fired tear gas and used stun grenades Wednesday to disperse garment workers protesting for higher wages, police and witnesses said. Hundreds of factories remained shut after days of protests disrupted the country’s garment industry, which earns about $40 billion a year from exports. Bangladesh has 2,500 garment factories. Workers are demanding a minimum monthly wage of 30,000 takas ($245), up from 12,500 takas. They say rising living costs and inflation have eroded their purchasing power. The industry employs about 4 million workers, mostly women from rural Bangladesh. After days of demonstrations in the capital, Dhaka, violence was reported in several industrial areas on its outskirts. In Fatullah, in Narayanganj district outside Dhaka, dozens of people were injured in clashes between protesters and police officers, according to media reports. Police fired tear gas and used stun grenades. Prothom Alo, Bangladesh’s largest Bengali-language daily newspaper, reported that police arrested several protesters in Fatullah. About 100 factories remain shut in Ashulia, in Savar near Dhaka, said Mominul Islam Bhuiyan, superintendent of Ashulia Industrial Police. Workers also blocked a major highway in Gazipur district, another major industrial hub. More than 10,000 police officers had been deployed in Dhaka’s Mirpur area, a center of recent protests, to maintain order, said Mahidul Islam, a joint police commissioner. The government has responded to the wage demands by forming a new wage board. The board’s chairman, Syed Azad Subhani, said workers would receive their first salaries under the new pay scale in January.

articles.title: North Korea says it tested air defense missile and staged cruise missile drill
articles.summary: State media said the air defense test confirmed the technical specifications and reliability of the missile’s new materials and multiple guidance modes.
articles.body: SEOUL, South Korea — North Korea test-fired a newly designed air defense missile system and staged a cruise missile strike drill Wednesday, state media reported Thursday. State news agency KCNA said the air defense test confirmed the technical specifications and reliability of the missile’s new materials and multiple guidance modes. It also confirmed the system’s ability to identify and track targets, the agency said. A subunit of North Korea’s long-range strategic cruise missile unit in the east also struck a virtual airport target in a drill Wednesday, KCNA said. The agency report confirmed a South Korean military statement Wednesday that Pyongyang had fired multiple missiles toward the sea from the Sondok area on the east coast. It was the fourth North Korean weapons launch in a month. A South Korean Defense Ministry official said Thursday that early detection data suggested the missiles could have been several different types. Images released by Pyongyang appeared to show the cruise missile carrying a cluster warhead, according to Shin Jong-woo, secretary general of the Korea Defense & Security Forum. He said the launch appeared intended to test how effectively the warhead could disperse a payload over a target area. Shin said the new air defense missile, first unveiled in November 2025, appears to have a guidance section resembling Russia’s S-400 surface-to-air missile.

articles.summary: The Supreme Court has ruled that the 24-hour period within which an accused person must be produced before a judicial magistrate begins from the time of
articles.body: The Supreme Court has ruled that the 24-hour period within which an accused person must be produced before a judicial magistrate begins from the time of detention, and not merely from the time of formal arrest.The court held that arrest and detention are effectively the same for the purpose of this constitutional safeguard, as a person's liberty is curtailed in both situations.It observed that “any attempt to draw an artificial distinction between detention and arrest is constitutionally unsustainable”.The Supreme Court also criticised several high courts for making an artificial distinction between arrest and detention. It clarified that the requirement to produce an accused person before the nearest magistrate within 24 hours applies from the point at which the person is first detained.In another significant observation, the court ruled that the fundamental rights of an accused person must take precedence over provisions of special laws in cases involving delays in trial and the grant of bail. Referring to contradictory verdicts on bail in cases under laws such as the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA), the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act and the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA), the court said the constitutional rights of an accused must be given priority.The court further observed that special laws cannot serve as a guide to interpreting the Constitution. articles.title: Why sausage rolls and veterinary fees vary in price across London
articles.summary: Location is not just the only factor on why prices differ across London, as Anna O'Neill finds out.
articles.body:
Have you ever wondered why the same item costs more or less depending on where in London you buy it?

Take a bog standard Greggs’ sausage roll for example. If you buy it in an outer London borough like Sutton, it costs £1.35. But if you buy it in central London you're likely to pay £1.60.

You might have guessed that the price difference, according to Greggs, is often about location.

"We use national pricing across most of our shops however, this can vary in certain locations where costs are higher than average, such as travel hubs," they told the BBC in a statement.

You might think the price of a pizza at the same chain would be the same wherever in London you eat it.

A Duo Romana pizza from Pizza Express costs £20.95 in Muswell Hill, north London.

But three miles (5km) further north in Southgate, the same pizza at Pizza Express costs a pound more.

And in central London the same pizza will set you back £22.95.

Consumer expert Helen Dewdney from the Complaining Cow website says that as well as higher costs in central London, the price difference can also be due to how convenient it is to get to the restaurant.

Southgate has a Tube station, Muswell Hill does not.

"It’s all about cashing in on convenience for people.

"One will be nearer a Tube, so they’re counting on people saying 'Oh, I'll just get a pizza on the way home'.

"Whereas another you might have to make a journey to it."

Other examples of cross-borough price variations include:

A Vue cinema ticket bought online costs £6.99 in Eltham, but £9.99 in Piccadilly or Angel, Islington

A blow dry at Rush hair salon costs from £45 in Kentish Town, north London but £40 in Ilford, east London

Fish, chips and a drink in Wetherspoons in Sidcup, south-east London costs £11.18 but the same meal in Camden Town, north London costs £12.77.

Also, petrol prices can vary from pump to pump at the same company and within as little as a mile (1.5km) radius.

A recent example from EG On the Move on the same day in London found these price variations:

Unleaded (E10): 171.9p – 177.9p per litre

Other forecourts also charge more or less if they are near a main road or a motorway or part of a supermarket for example.

For this Dewdney recommends downloading a price comparison app like petrolprices.com

"You can look at the distance as well as the price difference so you’re not driving too far away," she explained.

"It’s not always the nearest one that’s worth going to."

Recent changes to legislation mean that vets must publish a comprehensive price list for standard services but it does not necessarily follow that vets in a different practice at the same chain will have the same prices.

Vets for Pets in Pets At Home is a case in point.

In Pets At Home in Chingford, east London the Vets for Pets practice charges £136 for a rabbit castration including two follow-up consultations.

The same treatment at Vets For Pets in Pets At Home in Enfield, north London costs £70.

Consumer expert Helen Dewdney admits being surprised that the price can almost double from one practice to another.

"I think it's an interesting one, because they're saying it's a franchise and they can set their own prices.

"Although the government did bring in some changes for vets, it wasn't about capping the prices. It was just that they had to be more transparent," she explained.

Pets At Home said: "Vets for Pets practices are independently owned and operated, with practice owners having full clinical and day-to-day operational autonomy, including setting fees for delivering the high-quality care and services they provide.

"Pricing decisions are made locally and vary for many reasons including factors such as operating costs, staffing, facilities and the unique needs of the communities they serve.

"All costs are communicated clearly with clients ahead of any treatment or service being provided."

The company also said that veterinary practices had, like many businesses across the UK "experienced increased operating costs over the past year, including rises in energy, wages, medicines and other essential supplies".

It added: "These pressures are felt right across the sector, but practice teams work hard to keep costs as low as possible to ensure high-quality care is accessible and affordable for pet owners in their local communities."

Perhaps to shop around, and not to assume that prices at the same chain will be the same wherever you go, whether that be for veterinary care, your weekly shop, having your hair done or filling up the car.

Price comparison websites can be a useful tool, and it is worth remembering that just because goods may be from the same restaurant, supermarket or petrol station in a different area, prices may well vary.

Or as Dewdney summed up: "People have just got to do their research."

articles.title: Kate’s Knitalian: Artist turns Soho gallery into woolly deli
articles.summary: From spaghetti to Parma ham, everything at a new Soho exhibition is knitted, crocheted or embroidered.
articles.body:
A textile artist has turned a Soho gallery into an Italian restaurant and delicatessen - where everything on the menu is made of yarn.

Kate Jenkins's exhibition, Kate's Knitalian, has filled Air Contemporary in Ham Yard with knitted, embroidered and crocheted food.

Spaghetti, breadsticks, fish, fruit and veg are all on the shelves, and artwork is available to buy.

Jenkins's idea grew out of a year of eating.

She said: "Anything that I've eaten over the last year or so for my research has been Italian, so it just all has come together".

Tables are set up as if diners are about to arrive, while the walls are lined with slices of pizza, bottles of wine, ice cream and cicchetti, the small snacks served in Venetian bars.

There is also a pizza station where visitors can pick their own woolly toppings, from a margherita to a seafood marinara.

Jenkins said her favourite part of the show was the deli counter, hung with salami, Parma ham, lemons, chillies and strings of onions and garlic.

"All kind of knitted to scale and to perfection," she said. "It's been a joy to create."

The exhibition opened on 30 October and runs until 5 December. Entry is free and there is no need to book.

"You can just come, sit down or have a look around and just enjoy the wonders and delights of Italian cuisine," she said.

It is open from 10:00 to 18:00 GMT, Tuesday to Friday, and from 10:00 to 17:00 on Saturdays.

articles.title: Paul Chuckle prepares for stage debut at National Theatre
articles.summary: Paul Elliott, 79, says stage acting is "completely different" to the comedy of the Chuckle Brothers.
articles.body:
They say it's never to late to try something new and, after more than six decades in the entertainment industry, Paul Chuckle is about to prove that true.

Real name Paul Elliott, the 79-year-old, is preparing to appear in his first ever play, taking on the role of Mr Boo in Jim Carwright's The Rise and Fall of Little Voice at the National Theatre.

Elliott, from Rotherham, became a household name, alongside his late brother Barry, as one half of the haphazard Chuckle Brothers in children's TV show ChuckleVision, which ran from 1987 to 2009.

But now, after decades of playing for laughs, he is just weeks away from what he has described as his first ever "straight play".

Speaking to the BBC, he said: "63 years in the business and it's my first ever play, and, would you believe it, it's at the National Theatre - you can't write it.

"A young lad from East Herringthorpe, and now at the National.

Following the death of his brother in 2018 , Elliott said he was determined not to retire, and, in recent years, has turned his hand to a variety of new opportunities.

In 2025 he starred in a gangster movie, playing The Jackal in Fall to the Top, and later the same year appeared in Celebrity MasterChef.

In keeping with trying new things, he is also set to star as Monsignor O'Hara in a touring production of Sister Act at the end of 2027.

The Rise and Fall of Little Voice tells the story of as a shy girl who rarely ventures outside her bedroom, until her talent for imitating famous singers is recognised by a local promoter.

Elliott will perform alongside Silent Witness actress Francesca Mills, who will play the title role, and Waterloo Road star Jill Halfpenny, who will play her mother, Mari Hoff.

After a career including, TV, film, pantomime, circus and now regular DJ sets, he said adapting had been a challenge.

"It's the first show I've done in many, many years without saying 'to me, to you'.

"The lines are slowly sinking into my brain.

"I've found that hard. Barry and I ad libbed a lot when we were on stage.

"We had lots of fun, we used to fall about laughing at each other, but there's none of that, I've got to be word perfect.

"TV is easier. If you go wrong it's 'cut, do it again' but on stage you can't.

"When me and Barry worked together we loved things going wrong, but you can't do that in a live play."

One thing Elliott said he did know well ahead of stepping into the shoes of club promoter Mr Boo was the world of working men's clubs.

"Jim Cartwright, who wrote the play, he thought I would be perfect for the part of Mr Boo," he said.

"I was working in working men's clubs all my career, and he knew I was doing that.

"We did all the clubs in the North East, South Wales, Midlands, North Wales, wherever we could get the work, we grew up in working men's clubs. Not an easy life, may I tell you. Not an easy life.

"You never knew whether they're going to love you or hate you, and there was no real middle ground.

"They were either a fabulous audience or a terrible audience, or put it the other way, we were terrible or brilliant."

The Rise and Fall of Little Voice, directed by Robert Hastie, will run at the National Theatre in London from 2 December to 23 January, before heading to locations including Newcastle, Sheffield and Salford.

articles.title: Bradford's city music strategy announced
articles.summary: Nia Archives says the city has all the ingredients to become a powerhouse for musicians.
articles.body:
A new strategy to help musicians in Bradford achieve their potential has been backed by city star Nia Archives.

The Bradford-born singer-songwriter, DJ and producer, who spent her early years in the city before moving with her family to Leeds, has written a foreward for the Bradford District Music Strategy.

It was launched at Bradford Live over the weekend and is funded by Arts Council England's Grassroots Music Fund.

The strategy has set out an "ambitious vision" for the city to be recognised as one of the UK's most distinctive music districts but also how its musicians can get better access to venues, equipment and industry expertise.

In her foreward, Archives makes reference to her background and its influence on her work.

She said: "My Black British Jamaican heritage is ingrained in my music.

"I still take little pieces of what I was exposed to as a child and reinvent them in the music I make today.

"That's the thing about where you come from. You carry it with you."

She added: "I'd love Bradford to have more spaces where young people can get involved in music, where they can DJ, sing or rap, get work experience, meet people and find their own way into it.

"That's why I think it's so important that Bradford now has a plan for music.

"There is already so much here: the people, the talent, the music and that Bradford mentality of making something good out of what you have.

"Having a plan is a chance to build on that, create more opportunities for artists and musicians, and make sure the talent coming from Bradford gets heard."

Nan Brimble put together the strategy along with fellow artistic consultant Caroline Hansell.

She said: "I know that Nia Archives is a big supporter of Bradford anyway and she's done some work in the city before.

"We reached out to ask her to write the foreward to the strategy.

"She can put in that context of somebody that has grown up here, knows what its music scene is like and the inspiration that you get from being in Bradford."

Brimble said the hope was the city would eventually been seen as one of the UK's most distinctive music-producing areas.

She said: "It's based on the idea that there are lots of people in the city and the wider district in all genres of music doing amazing things.

"And there always has been. But actually we're better where we find coordination and have a bit of a plan.

"People find it hard to know what each other is doing.

"How can we make use of all these assets, like these amazing venues and spaces, or equipment.

"Or how can we support people who are working really hard to build careers in the music industry."

Last weekend's launch featured live performances from AllStar Entertainment, jazz band the Toby Brazier Trio, opera singer Natasha Agarwal and songwriter, producer and multi-instrumentalist MPTheHitMaker.

The strategy is backed by the British Phonographic Industry (BPI), the representative body for the UK's recorded music industry, and Bradford Live.

Bradford Culture Company, the charity that delivered Bradford 2025 UK City of Culture, is also supporting it.

articles.title: In 2015, Detroit's Claude P. Moore began building a ball from just two rubber bands; 11 years later, it weighed 11,578 pounds and broke a Guinness record, with volunteers using a crane to weigh the giant creation
articles.summary: Sometimes, something you might start without much thought can become a brilliant work later on in life. And Detroit’s Claude P.
articles.body: Sometimes, something you might start without much thought can become a brilliant work later on in life. And Detroit’s Claude P. Moore's experiment of building a ball from rubber bands is one such instance. In 2015, Detroit’s Claude P. Moore began winding together two rubber bands with no clear idea of how far the project would go. Eleven years later, that modest beginning had become an 11,578-pound rubber band ball, officially recognised by Guinness World Records as the largest ever made, according to Guinness World Records.The record was confirmed in August 2026 at Belle Isle in Detroit, Michigan, where a crane was used to weigh the enormous creation. Volunteers, family members and friends helped move the ball from its storage container and attach it to the crane, turning an unusual personal obsession into a public celebration of persistence. Read more details about it here:It began with two bandsMoore’s connection to rubber bands began long before the record attempt. As a child living with hemophilia, a rare and severe blood disorder, he spent considerable time in hospital waiting rooms and doctors’ offices, where he would occupy himself by twisting workplace rubber bands into small balls. Those early moments became the seed of a much larger ambition. Moore later said that coworkers encouraged him to build a massive version of the childhood toy, prompting him to revisit an idea that had stayed with him since middle school.He had already made a rubber band ball “as large as a chair” during his school years, only for it to be stolen by a classmate. Rather than discouraging him, that loss appears to have left the idea firmly in his mind, eventually leading him to wonder whether he could create the biggest ball the world had ever seen.Eleven years of workBuilding the ball was not a short-term project. Moore began in 2015 and continued adding rubber bands over more than a decade, eventually requiring a dedicated storage container after the creation outgrew his garage. The work demanded physical space, time and an extraordinary amount of patience. As the ball expanded, it became large enough to nearly touch the walls of the storage container, making it clear that the project had moved well beyond an ordinary hobby!Moore was not working entirely alone. He credited countless family members and friends, many of whom initially thought he was “crazy,” for helping him continue through the years of winding, storing and transporting the increasingly enormous object.Breaking the previous recordThe previous Guinness World Record for the largest rubber band ball stood at 9,032 pounds, or 4,097 kilograms, and was set by Joel Waul in Florida in 2008. Moore’s final creation surpassed that mark by a substantial margin.When officially weighed, Moore’s ball registered 11,578 pounds, equivalent to 5,251.69 kilograms. Guinness World Records described the weight as comparable to that of an elephant, a comparison that captures just how far the project had travelled from its two-band origin.The official ceremony took place at Belle Isle, where Guinness World Records adjudicator Chloe McCarthy oversaw the measurement process. Dozens of Moore’s friends, family members and coworkers attended, with many helping roll the ball out of its container and secure it to the crane.A crane and a crowdThe logistics of weighing the ball were almost as remarkable as the record itself. Volunteers had to move the massive object from storage, attach it safely to a crane and transport it to Belle Isle for the formal verification.As the crane lifted the ball into the air, McCarthy entered the crane cab and confirmed the record-breaking weight. The crowd reportedly erupted in cheers, with shouts of “Alright, Claudey!” filling the park as Moore accepted his certificate.McCarthy later said that seeing the ball in person was very different from viewing photographs of it. She praised Moore’s dedication, effort and advocacy, noting that many people would have abandoned a project requiring 11 years of sustained commitment.More than a recordFor Moore, the achievement carries personal meaning beyond the number on the scale. He has documented his experience with hemophilia in his 2021 book, 'My Life with Hemophilia', and spoke about that journey during the record event.He also distributed signed copies of the book to people attending the ceremony, using the moment to raise awareness of the condition that shaped much of his early life. The rubber band ball became both a record-breaking object and a visible symbol of resilience.Moore’s approach to the project reflected the same mindset he applies to life’s challenges. “The only excuse for failure is the lack of effort,” he told Guinness World Records, a philosophy that clearly guided him through more than a decade of work.What comes nextThe record has given Moore a major milestone, but he sees it as only one step in a larger vision. According to Guinness World Records, he hopes to continue pursuing ambitious goals, including working towards ending world hunger.That ambition may seem a long way from two rubber bands in a Detroit garage, but the ball itself proves the value of starting small and continuing consistently. What began as a way to pass time in medical waiting rooms became a record recognised around the world.Moore’s story is ultimately about more than rubber bands, weight or a certificate. It is about turning a childhood habit into a long-term commitment, inviting a community into the process and showing that extraordinary results can grow from remarkably ordinary beginnings.You use AI every day.
